विज्ञापन
खबरें लगातार पढ़ने के लिए अमर उजाला एप डाउनलोड करें

संवाद न्यूज एजेंसी
फरीदाबाद। शहर में बुधवार को सुबह से ही तेज धूप निकलने के कारण लोगों को गर्मी और उमस से राहत नहीं मिल सकी। पिछले कुछ दिनों से बारिश की उम्मीद लगाए बैठे शहरवासियों को बुधवार को भी निराशा हाथ लगी। मौसम विभाग की ओर से बारिश की संभावना जताई गई थी, लेकिन दिनभर बारिश नहीं हुई।
बुधवार को अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 30 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। सुबह से धूप निकलने के कारण बाजारों और सड़कों पर भी लोगों की अधिक भीड़ दिखाई नहीं दी। दोपहर के समय गर्मी बढ़ने से लोग जरूरी काम होने पर ही घरों से बाहर निकले। शहरवासियों का कहना है कि पिछले कई दिनों से मौसम में बदलाव और बारिश की उम्मीद बनी हुई है। आसमान में बादल दिखाई देने के बावजूद पर्याप्त बारिश नहीं हो रही है। बारिश नहीं होने से उमस और गर्मी का असर बना हुआ है। लोगों को उम्मीद है कि आने वाले दिनों में अच्छी बारिश होने से तापमान में गिरावट आएगी और उमस से राहत मिलेगी।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार बृहस्पतिवार को अधिकतम तापमान 34 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने की संभावना है। वहीं, विभाग ने 16 अगस्त तक बारिश की संभावना व्यक्त की है। बारिश होने की उम्मीद में शहरवासियों की नजरें आसमान पर टिकी हैं। बरसात के बाद लोगों को गर्मी से राहत मिल सकेगी।

(ग्लेन मैकग्रेगर, डरहम यूनिवर्सिटी)
डरहम, 12 अगस्त (द कन्वरसेशन) जापान के क्यूशू में हाल में आए भूकंप के बाद लोगों को बचाने की कोशिश कर रहे आपातकालीन कर्मियों को भीषण गर्मी का सामना भी करना पड़ा।
जुलाई के अंत में आए भूकंप में कम से कम 38 लोगों की मौत हो गई थी और हजारों लोग बेघर हो गये थे। भूकंप के बाद दिन का तापमान बढ़कर 30 डिग्री सेल्सियस के ऊपरी स्तर तक पहुंच गया और कुछ स्थानों पर पहली बार 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया। साथ ही हवा में नमी भी काफी अधिक थी।
अत्यधिक गर्मी आपातकालीन प्रतिक्रिया के लगभग हर पहलू को प्रभावित करती है। जापान के चार मुख्य द्वीपों में सबसे दक्षिणी द्वीप पर स्थित कुमामोतो क्षेत्र में 130 निकासी केंद्रों और अस्थायी आवासों में रह रहे लगभग 7,000 लोगों के लिए गर्म और उमस भरे मौसम से निर्जलीकरण (शरीर में पानी की कमी) और ‘हीटस्ट्रोक’ का खतरा बढ़ जाता है।
बुजुर्ग, शिशु और पुरानी बीमारियों से पीड़ित लोग विशेष रूप से इसके प्रति संवेदनशील होते हैं।
गर्मी के कारण लोगों के लिए सोना भी मुश्किल हो जाता है, खासकर तब जब एयर कंडीशनिंग (एसी) उपलब्ध न हो या बिजली की आपूर्ति बाधित हो गई हो। पर्याप्त नींद नहीं लेने से तनाव बढ़ सकता है और निर्णय लेने की क्षमता प्रभावित हो सकती है। आपातकालीन सेवाओं में लगे कर्मी भी इसी तरह प्रभावित होते हैं।
बचाव कार्य, मलबा हटाना और बुनियादी ढांचे की मरम्मत शारीरिक रूप से काफी मेहनत वाले काम हैं। अधिक तापमान से शारीरिक कार्यक्षमता कम हो जाती है, थकान बढ़ जाती है और बार-बार आराम करने की जरूरत पड़ती है, जिससे राहत और बचाव कार्यों की गति धीमी हो सकती है।
इन प्रभावों का असर स्वास्थ्य के अलावा अन्य चीजों पर भी पड़ता है। क्षतिग्रस्त जल ढांचे के कारण पीने के पानी की मांग बढ़ जाती है, ठीक उस समय जब पानी की आपूर्ति सीमित हो सकती है। इसी दौरान, जारी बिजली कटौती के बीच ठंडक के लिए बिजली की मांग बढ़ जाती है।
कुछ इलाकों में पानी की आपूर्ति बाधित हो गई है और बिजली कटौती के कारण ठंडक देने वाले उपकरणों का इस्तेमाल सीमित हो गया है, जिससे निकासी केंद्रों में बहुत अधिक गर्मी हो गई है। ये परिस्थितियां एक दूसरी आपात स्थिति पैदा करती हैं, जिस पर भूकंप की तुलना में बहुत कम ध्यान दिया जाता है, लेकिन इसका जनस्वास्थ्य और रबचाव एवं पुनर्वास कार्यों पर गहरा असर पड़ सकता है।
वर्ष 2026 की परिस्थितियां उन परिस्थितियों से बहुत अलग हैं, जब कुमामोतो में पिछली बार अप्रैल 2016 में बड़े भूकंप आए थे।
वर्ष 2016 के कुमामोतो भूकंप ने व्यापक तबाही मचाई थी। हालांकि, उस समय अप्रैल का तापमान अपेक्षाकृत सामान्य था।
कुमामोतो का भूकंप दिखाता है कि अत्यधिक गर्मी आपदा के जोखिम को कई गुना बढ़ाने वाला एक बड़ा कारक बन सकती है।
कुमामोतो में आये भूकंप से पता चलता है कि आपदा से निपटने की क्षमता अब केवल मजबूत बुनियादी ढांचा बनाने या भूकंप-रोधी डिजाइन में सुधार करने तक सीमित नहीं है।
जलवायु परिवर्तन के कारण जब अत्यधिक गर्मी की घटनाओं की आवृत्ति और तीव्रता बढ़ रही है, तब आपातकालीन स्थितियों की तैयारी करने वालों को इसे भी अपनी योजना में शामिल करना होगा।
जैसे-जैसे दुनिया में लू की घटनाएं बढ़ रही हैं, अत्यधिक तापमान साल के सबसे गर्म समय में आपदा के बाद राहत एवं बचाव कार्यों के लिए नयी चुनौतियां पैदा करेगा।
(द कन्वरसेशन) देवेंद्र संतोष

उत्तरी और मध्य क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी जारी है, जबकि मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्रों में दोपहर और शाम के बाद छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ने की संभावना है। अगले 10 दिनों (12 अगस्त, 2026 की रात से 22 अगस्त, 2026 तक) के मौसम पूर्वानुमान में लू और वर्षा दोनों के पैटर्न में महत्वपूर्ण बदलाव दिखाई दे रहे हैं।
12 अगस्त, 2026 से 22 अगस्त, 2026 तक 10 दिनों का मौसम पूर्वानुमान: भीषण गर्मी के साथ-साथ गरज के साथ बारिश।
12 अगस्त, 2026 से 22 अगस्त, 2026 तक देशव्यापी मौसम पूर्वानुमान: मध्य और उत्तरी वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी जारी रहेगी, जबकि मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में स्थानीय स्तर पर भारी बारिश के लिए तैयार रहना चाहिए।
12 अगस्त की रात से 14 अगस्त, 2026 तक का मौसम पूर्वानुमान

articles.title: उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी जारी है; तापमान कब कम होगा? - Vietnam.vn

articles.full_text:
वीडियो देखें :
उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी जारी है; तापमान कब कम होगा?
उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में व्यापक लू का प्रकोप जारी रहेगा, जहां तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है, इसके बाद अगस्त के मध्य से तापमान में गिरावट शुरू हो जाएगी।
12 अगस्त की शाम को, राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान और जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र की मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता फुओंग ची ने उत्तरी और मध्य वियतनाम में लू के विकास के बारे में जानकारी प्रदान की।
इसी के चलते, हाल के दिनों में वियतनाम के उत्तरी और मध्य क्षेत्रों के अधिकांश हिस्सों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ रही है। अगले कुछ दिनों तक यह गर्म और उमस भरा मौसम जारी रहने की संभावना है।
विशेष रूप से उत्तरी क्षेत्र में, कल (13 अगस्त) भी भीषण गर्मी की लहर जारी रहेगी। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा, जबकि कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है।
14 अगस्त तक, लू की तीव्रता पहले की तुलना में कुछ कम हो गई थी। हालांकि, दिन का अधिकतम तापमान अब भी 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गया था, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह 36 डिग्री से भी अधिक था। पूर्वानुमानों के अनुसार, उत्तरी वियतनाम में यह लू 15 अगस्त से समाप्त होने की संभावना है।
मध्य क्षेत्र में 13 से 14 अगस्त तक भीषण गर्मी की लहरें चलेंगी। इस गर्मी की लहर का असर थान्ह होआ से दा नांग तक के क्षेत्रों, क्वांग न्गाई से डाक लक तक के प्रांतों के पूर्वी हिस्सों और खान्ह होआ प्रांतों पर पड़ेगा।
इन क्षेत्रों में तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहता है, कुछ स्थानों पर तो भीषण गर्मी पड़कर तापमान 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो जाता है। 15 अगस्त से मध्य वियतनाम में लू की लहर धीरे-धीरे कम होने लगेगी।
मौसम पूर्वानुमानकर्ता फुओंग ची ने बताया कि सतह की स्थितियों (कंक्रीट, डामर) के आधार पर वास्तविक रूप से महसूस किया गया बाहरी तापमान पूर्वानुमानित तापमान से 1-3 डिग्री अधिक हो सकता है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी ने चेतावनी दी है, "दिन में सबसे तेज धूप सुबह 11 बजे से शाम 5 बजे तक रहती है। बाहर यात्रा करने या काम करने वाले लोगों को अपनी सेहत की रक्षा करने और गर्मी से होने वाली थकावट के खतरे से बचने के लिए धूप से बचाव के सामान साथ रखने चाहिए और पर्याप्त पानी पीना चाहिए।"

articles.title: पंजाब में कल बारिश का अलर्ट नहीं, कुछ जगहों पर हो सकती है बूंदाबांदी; तापमान चढ़ने से बढ़ी गर्मी और उमस - Jagran
articles.search_term: ("पारा चढ़ा" OR "पारा पहुंचा" OR तापमान OR "तापमान बढ़ा" OR "रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी" OR "डिग्री सेल्सियस" OR "पारा उबला" OR "अधिकतम तापमान" OR "तापमान 40 पार" OR "तापमान 45 पार" OR "तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
पंजाब में कल बारिश का अलर्ट नहीं, कुछ जगहों पर हो सकती है बूंदाबांदी; तापमान चढ़ने से बढ़ी गर्मी और उमस
पंजाब में वीरवार को कोई अलर्ट जारी नहीं किया गया। हालांकि कुछ जिलों में कहीं-कहीं बारिश की संभावना है। अधिकतम तापमान में औसतन 4.6 डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी हु ...और पढ़ें
HighLights
पंजाब के कुछ जिलों में हल्की बारिश की संभावना है।
राज्य के औसत तापमान में 4.6 डिग्री की वृद्धि हुई।
आने वाले दिनों में उमस बढ़ने के स्पष्ट आसार हैं।
डिजिटल डेस्क, अमृतसर। पंजाब में वीरवार को मानसून का असर कमजोर रहने के बावजूद कई जिलों में कहीं-कहीं बारिश होने की संभावना है। मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार प्रदेश में किसी भी जिले के लिए कोई मौसम चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। हालांकि, उत्तरी और कुछ मध्य तथा दक्षिणी जिलों में अलग-अलग स्थानों पर बारिश हो सकती है।
मौसम विभाग के जिलेवार पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार पठानकोट, गुरदासपुर, होशियारपुर, नवांशहर, रूपनगर, मोहाली, फतेहगढ़ साहिब, बठिंडा, मुक्तसर, फाजिल्का और मानसा में कुछ स्थानों पर बारिश होने की संभावना है। वहीं अमृतसर, तरनतारन, कपूरथला, जालंधर, लुधियाना, मोगा, फिरोजपुर, फरीदकोट, बरनाला, संगरूर और पटियाला में छिटपुट बारिश के आसार हैं।

तापमान में 4.6 डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी
मंगलवार के मुकाबले बुधवार को पंजाब के औसत अधिकतम तापमान में 4.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की गई। हालांकि यह सामान्य के आसपास रहा। प्रदेश में सबसे अधिक 37.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापमान भाखड़ा बांध क्षेत्र में दर्ज किया गया।
पटियाला में 36.6, नवांशहर में 35.5, लुधियाना और बठिंडा में 35, फतेहगढ़ साहिब में 34.9, होशियारपुर में 34.8, फरीदकोट में 34, अमृतसर और जालंधर में 34.2 डिग्री तापमान रहा। संगरूर में अधिकतम तापमान 33.5 डिग्री दर्ज किया गया।

कुछ स्थानों पर हुई हल्की बारिश
पिछले 24 घंटे के दौरान पंजाब में बारिश बहुत कम रही। थेन बांध क्षेत्र में 0.5 मिलीमीटर और रोपड़ में एक मिलीमीटर बारिश दर्ज की गई। बाकी अधिकांश स्थानों पर बारिश दर्ज नहीं हुई।
खबरें और भी
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार अगले कुछ दिनों में बारिश की गतिविधियां बढ़ने के आसार हैं। ऐसे में तापमान बढ़ने के साथ उमस भी लोगों को परेशान कर सकती है। बुधवार को बारिश होने वाले क्षेत्रों में कुछ समय के लिए गर्मी से राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है।

articles.title: Five foods that can help keep children hydrated during a heatwave - The Conversation

articles.full_text:
“Have another drink.” It can become a familiar refrain for parents during a heatwave, particularly when a child is busy playing and has little interest in stopping for a glass of water.
Keeping up fluid intake becomes more important as temperatures rise because heat increases water loss, particularly through sweating. But a child’s fluid intake does not have to come solely from a cup or water bottle – the water in food also counts.
That contribution can be substantial. An analysis of Australian dietary data found that moisture in food supplied 29% of total water intake among children and adolescents. And research involving children aged four to ten found that those who ate more fruit and vegetables tended to have better measures of hydration.
Water-rich foods should supplement regular drinks rather than replace them. But if getting children to drink enough feels like a battle, food can provide another way of adding fluid to their day.
Here are five options.
1. Watermelon and other juicy fruits
Many fruits and vegetables are around 90% water, which is why foods such as watermelon, strawberries, oranges, peaches and melon can contribute to fluid intake.
There is child-specific evidence for this. In a study of 442 children aged four to ten, solid fruit and vegetables provided around 12% of their total water intake. Children who ate more fruit and vegetables also had better measures of hydration.
So offering watermelon, berries or sliced fruit during hot weather provides another source of water alongside regular drinks.
2. Homemade ice lollies
If repeatedly offering a drink is getting you nowhere, changing how it is served may help.
Reusable ice-lolly moulds can be filled with milk, yoghurt, blended fruit or diluted fruit juice. Water consumed through foods and other fluids still contributes to total water intake, so a homemade lolly offers another way to provide fluid.
Making them yourself also gives you control over the ingredients. Although homemade lollies are not automatically healthier, you can choose what goes into each lolly, making it easier to create lower-sugar versions while also involving children in deciding which combinations they would like to try.
3. Cucumber, tomatoes and peppers
Fruit may be the obvious choice when you think about juicy foods, but vegetables can contribute to water intake too.
Cucumber has a particularly high water content, while many other vegetables also contain a large proportion of water. More importantly, research in children has directly linked greater fruit and vegetable consumption with higher water intake and better hydration.
Cucumber, tomatoes or pepper strips can be served alone or alongside familiar foods such as hummus or cream cheese. They also work well in lunchboxes and snack plates when nobody particularly wants to cook or eat a large hot meal.
4. Yoghurt, milk and dairy foods
Fruit and vegetables are not the only foods that can add fluid to the diet. Milk and dairy products also contribute to children’s overall intake of water and nutrients.
In British children, yoghurt consumption has been associated with higher intakes of nutrients including calcium, iodine and riboflavin. The study was observational, so it cannot show that eating yoghurt caused those differences, but it demonstrates that yoghurt can fit into a nutrient-rich diet.
Yoghurt can be eaten cold with fruit, blended into a smoothie or frozen into a lolly. Milk can also contribute directly to fluid intake, and research comparing different drinks has shown that milk can support fluid balance.
Fortified dairy alternatives are another option, although their nutritional composition varies between products.
5. Build a hydrating ‘picky tea’
You do not have to serve each water-rich food separately. A snack-style meal can bring several together.
A plate could contain melon or berries, cucumber and pepper sticks, yoghurt, cheese, hummus and bread or crackers. Fruit, vegetables and other moisture-containing foods can collectively make a meaningful contribution to total water intake.
It can also be worth being flexible about what constitutes dinner during exceptionally hot weather.
On holiday recently, my nephew asked for a bowl of cereal for dinner because he did not fancy anything else. I thought that was a perfectly sensible choice. It was cool, familiar, contained milk and, crucially, he wanted to eat it.
Would I suggest cereal for dinner every night? Probably not. But we do not usually have heatwaves every night in the UK, although recent summers sometimes seem determined to test that proposition.
Food helps, but keep offering drinks
Water-rich foods can contribute appreciably to children’s total water intake, but studies suggest that differences in how much people drink still account for most of the variation in overall water consumption. So fruit, yoghurt and ice lollies are useful additions rather than replacements for regular drinks.
Parents should also take possible dehydration seriously. A study of dehydration in children found that no single symptom is sufficient to diagnose it reliably, so a combination of changes in a child’s appearance, behaviour and fluid intake may be more informative than watching for one particular sign.
The useful principle is simple: keep offering drinks, but remember that hydration can arrive on a plate as well as in a glass.

articles.title: UK weather: Burnham to chair Cobra meeting on extreme heat as temperatures surge again - BBC

articles.full_text:
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will chair a meeting of the government's emergency Cobra committee on Wednesday to discuss the UK's response to the extreme heat, as temperatures are set to soar again.
A No 10 spokesperson said the government understood firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather.
This week's latest heatwave comes as more areas in England were placed under drought status on Monday and firefighters continue to battle a significant wildfire in the New Forest in Hampshire.
The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning, external for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible
It comes as the record for the number of days reaching 30C in any year in the UK has been broken, according to the Met Office, with Sunday the 35th day of the year so far.
The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.
It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.
A spokesperson for No 10 said this summer was proving "challenging" in the UK, particularly for "firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units".
"We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment," they said.
The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.
Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.
This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.
It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.
On Monday, drought officials declared 71.3% of England in drought, meaning there are a total of 45 million people now living in a drought area, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.
Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August, and 458 in July, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.
A fire in the New Forest has been burning since Sunday, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood.
Last week, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS should be "preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter".
She told LBC Radio plans were in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E.
On Tuesday, the Met Office said this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, with the mean temperature currently at 16.48C set to surpass the figure set just last year.
This is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the Cobra meeting was just a first step, and a "climate emergency" had led to hundreds of deaths and was "stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit".
He called for "concrete action" and said he looked forward to hearing how Burnham intended to "prepare for the threats to come".
Amber heat health alerts also in force
The UK's Health Security Agency has also issued amber heat health alerts, which cover the whole of England.
Heat health alerts warn the public and medical professionals when periods of hot or cold weather pose a threat to health.
They warn that significant impacts are likely across social and health care, including a rise in deaths.
The alerts are in place until Friday evening.
When will the heatwave end?
This heatwave should be shorter lived than others so far this summer with temperatures starting to feel noticeably cooler over the weekend.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will not experience the same extreme heat as southern England, although eastern parts of Northern Ireland, southern and eastern Scotland will still see temperatures well above the heatwave threshold.
They will be notably above average for mid-August and the humidity is likely to intensify on Wednesday night into Thursday.
Some places could reach the mid to high 20s Celsius on Wednesday - when a typical August daytime temperature would generally be in the high teens to low 20s.
Western Scotland and western parts of Northern Ireland are likely to remain somewhat cooler due to cloud and occasional rain moving in from the Atlantic.
While confidence in the details remains low, this could open the door for showers and perhaps some prolonged spells of rain.
To alleviate drought though, months of above-average rainfall is needed.
What has caused the summer heat?
The persistence of high-pressure weather systems over recent months has been unusual but this is the type of summer scientists have warned about due to climate change.
As average temperatures rise – mainly due to the burning of fossil fuels around the world – hot weather becomes much more likely and more intense.
While temperatures will continue to vary from year to year, scientists warn that summers will keep getting hotter on average as carbon emissions continue to heat up the planet.
This means future heatwaves will be able to reach even higher temperatures than the same weather systems of the past.

articles.title: Too hot to think? Why extreme heat can affect how well our brain works - The Conversation
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Ever feel that the arrival of summer sun makes you feel a bit dopey? You wouldn’t be the only one. Soaring temperatures are known for their ability to slow our thought processes, making even everyday tasks seem like a baffling ordeal.
But what is actually happening inside our heads when the heat is on? The explanation appears to lie in the extra work our brain and body have to do to keep us cool.
The brain and body are in constant conversation. When outdoor temperatures change, thermoreceptors which sit near the surface of the skin send signals to the hypothalamus – the brain’s temperature regulation centre.
When things become too hot or cold, the hypothalamus co-ordinates a series of responses to bring body temperature back towards normal (around 37°C). Keeping the core temperature at this level is critical for metabolism, activity of enzymes and many other essential body functions.
Being commander-in-chief of temperature regulation means that the brain becomes rather occupied when having to consistently regulate your temperature.
In hot weather, this means cooling the body down by switching on mechanisms that allow heat to radiate from the surface. This includes diverting blood to the skin, flattening skin hairs and sweating.
These responses are governed by nervous pathways that link the brain to blood vessels and sweat glands. This allows it to fine-tune the amount of heat the body sheds.
But the additional demand that keeping cool places on the brain may therefore leave less capacity for it to perform cognitive tasks which require sustained thought and attention.
This becomes particularly noticeable if you’re also exercising or exerting yourself at the same time. This is because working muscles and metabolism generate heat, which places additional strain on the body and brain’s cooling mechanisms.
Our neurons (nerve cells) may also start to function differently with rising heat. Neurons rely on the flow of electrical currents and the release of chemical neurotransmitters to function. These processes depend upon enzymes, proteins and the movement of charged ions in and out of the neuron – all of which are sensitive to temperature.
Although the brain is normally able to compensate and keep up with these demands, past a certain point the finely controlled balance becomes disrupted. This alters the way neurons fire and communicate with each other, which can affect processes such as memory, decision-making and concentration.
Another potential complication to consider is dehydration, which commonly occurs in hot weather as we lose more fluid in sweat. Failing to replace fluid losses adequately means additional strain is placed on the cardiovascular system as it tries to supply the skin and organs – including the brain – with blood.
Like many other organs, the brain is over 70% water. Even modest dehydration can result in impairment to attention, reaction times and short-term memory.
This is because dehydration can affect the brain in several ways. It can reduce cerebral blood flow, alter the way that neurons function and even affect the delicate balance of electrolytes needed for normal activity – all of which impact how well our brain works.
Another important consideration is not just how brain and body respond to heat in the moment, but also in the aftermath when they rest and recuperate – namely, through sleep. In hotter weather, it can become increasingly difficult to sleep. And, if you do manage to doze off, the time spent in deeper, restorative sleep may also be short-lived.
In disrupting sleep, hot weather adds another contribution to brain fog: inadequate sleep impairs attention, memory and thinking – furthering the effects of heat on cognitive performance.
Keeping cool
The degree to which the heat affects our thinking will probably vary between people. Some may cope well, whereas others may find difficulty in doing complex cognitive tasks or simple, everyday activities. This will be due in part to individual differences in physiology and heat tolerance.
Perception matters, too. Even a relatively small dip in attention or processing speed can feel much more dramatic when we notice ourselves struggling with something that would usually come easily.
Try not to be hard on yourself if this happens. Take a moment to chill, rehydrate and reclaim your thoughts.
You can fend off some of this summer brain fog by keeping yourself cool as best as you can. Simple measures such as cool clothing, bedding and taking regular breaks from heat exposure do work wonders. Good fluid intake is also paramount to making sure both body and brain stay hydrated.
While it’s frustrating when our brains just don’t feel like they’re firing on all cylinders on hot days, just remember that it’s only a temporary blip. And one that should start to ease off as we cool down.

Hot weather set to continue advice to help residents stay safe
Dorset is experiencing another period of very hot weather, with temperatures expected to remain high over the coming days.
Hot weather can affect anyone's health, but older people, young children, people with long-term health conditions and those who live alone may be particularly at risk. Taking a few simple precautions can help keep you, your family and your neighbours safe.
During heatwaves, more people than usual get seriously ill or die. When hot weather hits, make sure it does not harm you or anyone you know.
The main health risks during hot weather include:
- not drinking enough water and becoming dehydrated. More information about this can be found on the NHS information dehydration webpage
- overheating, which can make symptoms worse for people who already have problems with their heart or breathing
- Heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Information about the symptoms and what to do about them can be found on the NHS heat exhaustion and heatstroke webpages.
How to stay safe in hot weather
Keep out of the heat if you can. If you have to go outside, stay in the shade especially between 11am and 3pm, wear sunscreen, a hat and light clothes, and avoid exercise or activity that makes you hotter.
Cool yourself down. Have cold food and regular cold drinks. Drink plenty of water and other fluids. Try to avoid too much alcohol or drinks containing caffeine.
Keep your living space cool. Close windows, curtains and blinds during the day and open them at night when the temperature outside has gone down. Electric fans can help when indoor temperatures are below 35°C. Check the temperature of rooms, particularly where vulnerable people live or sleep, and check regularly on family members, friends and neighbours who may be at greater risk. For more information, visit Heat - GOV.UK
Water Safety
When temperatures rise, many people head to the coast, rivers or lakes to cool down. If you are planning to swim outdoors, follow these simple safety tips.
Check that the water you want to visit is classified as bathing waters. Many rivers are not classified as such and may cause illness due to water borne infections. Check for bathing water at Bathing water quality
Before you enter the water, assess the conditions. If the water is too rough for swimming, don’t get in. Know your limits – depending on the conditions, you may need to swim less or closer to the bank or shore. The temperature of the air and water is also important – the colder the water and air temperature, the quicker you will cool down. So, the colder it is, the less time you should spend in the water.
When swimming in open water, it's important to enter the water slowly and give your body time to adjust to the temperature. Never jump or dive straight in, as this could cause cold water shock. Details on this and other water safety tips can be found at RNLI Water Safety - The Dangers Of Cold Water Shock
If you find yourself struggling in the water, remember to Float to Live. Tilt your head back, relax and try to control your breathing until help arrives or you can reach safety. Details can be found at Float To Live – What To Do If You Fall In Water
Heath fires and countryside safety
When you are out and about enjoying the countryside, there are some things you can do to protect our beautiful surroundings and keep you safe.
Steps you can take to avoid starting a wildfire:
- Avoid having open fires or using barbecues in the countryside.
- Barbecues and campfires are banned in many country parks, campsites and open spaces. Make sure you check what is and isn’t allowed where you are, and follow the rules.
- Extinguish smoking materials properly, and don’t throw cigarette ends on the ground or out of car windows – take your litter home.
If you see a fire in the countryside, report it immediately to the Fire & Rescue Service. Early detection can prevent it from developing into a large wildfire incident.
There is more information about reporting fires and the devastating effects of wildfires at Dorset & Wiltshire Fire and Rescue Service | Heath fires and countryside safety
While many people enjoy spending time outdoors during warm weather, it's important to take extra care during periods of extreme heat. Looking after yourself and checking on others can help prevent serious illness and save lives.

Temperatures might hit 36°C in parts of Taiwan, while the nation’s southwest faces the threat of heavy rain, with unstable weather expected over the next few days, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The CWA issued an “orange” heat alert for parts of Taipei and New Taipei City yesterday, indicating that temperatures could reach 38°C or exceed 36°C for three consecutive days.
A “yellow” heat alert — warning of highs of 36°C — was issued for parts of Taoyuan, as well as Changhua, Hualien and Taitung counties.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
As of 1:42pm yesterday, the highest daytime temperatures were 36.9°C in New Taipei City’s Sindian District (新店), 36.2°C in Taitung County’s Luye Township (鹿野) and 36.0°C in other parts of New Taipei City and Taitung.
The CWA also issued a heavy rain advisory, warning that southwesterly winds could bring short-duration downpours to Tainan and Kaohsiung, as well as Chiayi city and county, and Pingtung County, including the Hengchun Peninsula.
The agency issued a strong wind advisory for Green Island (綠島), and Hsinchu city and county, warning of sustained winds of 41 to 51kph (six on the Beaufort scale) and 63 to 75kph (eight on the Beaufort scale).
Independent meteorologist Wu Der-rong (吳德榮) said forecasts showed that southwesterly winds would bring moisture from the South China Sea through tomorrow, making atmospheric conditions unstable.
Intermittent rain in windward areas in southwestern Taiwan are expected through tomorrow, while localized afternoon thunderstorms are expected in central and northern Taiwan, some of which might bring heavy rainfall, Wu said in an online weather column.
Outside of rainy periods, daytime temperatures would be high, especially in eastern Taiwan, and parts of central and northern Taiwan, he said.
From Saturday through Aug. 21, seasonal winds are expected to weaken and give way to a broad low-pressure system near Taiwan, Wu said.
Although moisture would remain abundant, the main weather threat is expected to shift to frequent afternoon convective storms capable of producing lightning, strong winds and intense short-term rainfall, he said, urging the public to monitor short-term weather advisories.
Meanwhile, the CWA said that Tropical Storm Nangka formed at 8am yesterday over waters south of Iwo Jima after strengthening from a tropical depression.
The storm is forecast to move northeast and not affect Taiwan, the agency said.
